1:
Job's reply to Eliphaz opens the long central duel of the book, and the witnesses gather first around the bare fact that he answers at all, and the temper in which he does it. The reformed John Gill dwells on Job's restraint: though Eliphaz thought his speech unanswerable, the fruit of strict and diligent inquiry, Job had waited with patience until the whole discourse was finished, giving no interruption though much in it was provoking; and now he claims no more than every man's right, to answer for himself when his character and his good name — better than precious ointment — are under attack, a right the laws of all civilized nations allow. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same forbearance as a rule for hearers: those who would make an impartial judgment of a discourse must hear it out and take it entire; Job heard Eliphaz patiently to the end, and only then makes his reply, in which, Henry says, he speaks very feelingly.

The latin-fathers Gregory the Great turns to the deeper wound. Some men are more hurt by reproaches than by scourges, for the tortures of speech often assail us worse than any pains, and while they provoke us to rise in our own vindication they lay us low in impatience. So, that no kind of temptation might be lacking to blessed Job, not only did scourges strike him from above, but the sayings of his friends galled him, sorer than scourges, that the soul of the holy man, driven hither and thither, might burst forth in wrath and haughtiness of speech and defile the purity he had lived in. Yet, Gregory insists, when touched by the scourges Job gave thanks, and when galled with words he answered aright; there were but a few things mixed with his words which, in the judgment of men, might seem to overstep the limits of patience — and even these must be weighed by the sentence of the Most High Judge, who had himself called Job a perfect and upright man in Job 1:8.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the emotional key of the whole chapter. Job replies with the despair of a man who has been baulked of sympathy just where he hoped to find it; we must not look here for the formal reply of a logical argument, for Eliphaz has so misjudged his case that he is felt to be neither worthy of a direct answer nor able to receive one. It is enough for Job to reiterate his complaint and to long for someone who can enter into it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke frames the movement of the reply as a whole: Job vindicates himself, showing that his great affliction is the true cause of the complaining that has made life a burden to him, before he turns, later in the chapter, to reproach the friends for offering reproaches where he had looked for consolation. The voices do not divide; they set the stage for a sufferer who will answer, but out of an anguish his comforters have not begun to measure.
2:
The reply proper begins with a wish framed as a courtroom weighing — "Oh that my grief were thoroughly weighed" — and the witnesses turn at once to the disputed noun and the image of the balances. The reformed John Gill notes the intensive Hebrew, "in weighing weighed," that is, most nicely and exactly weighed; and he lays out how much lies under the single English word. It may be Job's grief of heart, or his "wrath" and "anger" — not against Eliphaz, but the resentment his afflictions had stirred, which broke out in hot passionate speech and got him blamed as foolish — or his "complaint," the groans he made, or the "impatience" he was charged with. Whichever it be, his wish is that it might be weighed by kind and judicious persons, men of moderation, who together with his afflictions would set it in the scale and make large allowance for it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the two words that the wish sets against each other. "Vexation" (kaas) is the very thing Eliphaz had reproached him with in Job 5:2; Job asks that this vexation be laid in one scale and his suffering in the other, and weighed together. The word they read for that suffering comes from a root meaning to gape or yawn, and signifies properly a hiatus, a yawning gulf, a chasm — hence some dreadful calamity; and the verb is a picture of lifting the balance-beam so that the heavier pan sinks. The wish, they say, is that if the friends but understood the matter it would then be manifest how the weight lay.

The wesleyan-arminian voices hear in the balances a cry for justice. Adam Clarke reads Job as asking to be dealt with according to strict justice: let his sins, if they can be proved, be weighed against his sufferings; and if that cannot be done, then let his sufferings and his complainings be weighed together, and it will be seen that, bitter as the complaint has been, it is a small thing beside the distress that occasioned it. John Wesley glosses "my grief" as the cause of his grief, and "weighed" as fully understood and duly considered, and hears beneath the wish the longing for an impartial arbiter: "O that I had an equal judge, that would understand my case," and set his complaint in one scale together with any other most heavy thing in the other. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same thought: unable fully to describe his calamity, and doubting the friends would own it, Job would gladly appeal to a third person who had just weights and just balances, to weigh his grief and his calamity with an impartial hand. The witnesses do not divide; together they make the verse a plea to be measured before being condemned.
3:
Job completes the weighing with a hyperbole — his grief would prove "heavier than the sand of the sea" — and the witnesses measure both the image and the broken clause that follows it. The reformed John Gill presses the figure hard: all sand is heavy in itself, the sand freshly taken from the sea heavier still for the water in it, and how much more the sand of all the seas of the world; by this exaggeration Job means that his affliction is a most intolerable, insupportable burden. Yet Gill will not let the complaint stand unqualified. The afflictions of God's people are light when set against what their sins deserve, against the torments of hell, against the sufferings of Christ in their stead, and against the eternal weight of glory; but in themselves, to flesh and blood, they press hard and are heavy indeed, unless the everlasting arms are put underneath.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the comparison into two ideas at once: the sand of the sea is beyond counting for number and beyond estimating for weight, and Job's calamity is both — past reckoning and past measuring. John Wesley adds that sea-sand is heavier than dry sand, and turns to the closing words: to be "swallowed up" is to have voice and spirit fail, so that Job cannot find or utter words sufficient to express his sorrow and misery. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same clause in the same key — his words are "swallowed up," that is, words are useless and powerless to express what he feels.

It is over this last clause that a quiet difference of rendering opens. Where the others hear Job confessing that language sinks under the weight, the other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, render the line "therefore my words are rash" — not that speech fails him, but that the very hugeness of the burden is what makes his words unmeasured and wild, and so, in advance, excuses their vehemence. The two readings are not far apart in the end, for both trace the disorder of Job's speech back to the disproportion of his suffering: whether his words are drowned and lost, or driven to rashness, the cause is one, that no scale the friends possess has yet been made to bear so great a grief. The witnesses leave the verse having turned a single crushed phrase into Job's whole apology for the manner of his complaint.
4:
Now Job names the true source of his anguish — "the arrows of the Almighty are within me" — and the witnesses agree that the sharpest wound is not in his body or estate but in his spirit, struck from above. The reformed John Gill allows that the arrows might mean outward calamities, the famine, pestilence, and lightning that Scripture elsewhere calls God's arrows, all of which had found Job; but he judges the deeper reference to be the inward distresses and anguish of mind that attended them, a keen sense of the divine displeasure, as in David's like complaint. These arrows came suddenly, secretly, and swiftly, stuck fast, and wounded to the quick, and Job feels them as shot from the bow of God — and, worse, of God not dealing with him as a father.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses dwell on the burning poison. Adam Clarke sees a plain reference to wounds made by poisoned arrows and the raging fever they breed — a thirst that dries up every moisture, inflames the blood, and ends in terror and death; and he adduces the saying of Aaly, that if the canopy of heaven were a bow, the earth its cord, calamities the arrows, mankind the mark, and Almighty God the unerring Archer, then the sons of Adam could flee for protection only unto the Lord. John Wesley reads the arrows as dipped in God's wrath, as barbarous nations dipped theirs in poison, that they might not only pierce but burn up the vital parts; the poison "drinketh up" the spirit, exhausting and consuming the soul, and the terrors stand "in array" like a numerous army invading on every side. Here, Wesley adds, Job was an eminent type of Christ, who in his passion complained most of the sufferings of his soul — "now is my soul troubled" in John 12:27, and the cry of dereliction in Matt. 27:46.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the same point the crown of the verse: it is an instance of God's power above any man's that he can with his arrows reach the very soul; trouble of mind is the sorest trouble, and a wounded spirit who can bear? Over one clause the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the rendering: the Authorised "the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit" is ambiguous, and it is rather "the poison whereof my spirit imbibeth" — Job's own soul drinking in the venom; and "do set themselves in array" pictures the terrors of God like hosts marshalling themselves for battle. Keil and Delitzsch render the line the same way, "the terrors of Eloah set themselves in array against me," so that the sufferer stands besieged. The witnesses do not divide on the substance: the deadliest stroke of all is the felt wrath of the God he loves.
5:
Job defends the very fact of his complaining with a homely question drawn from the farmyard — "Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder?" — and the witnesses read the two beasts as his argument in miniature. The reformed John Gill draws out the logic: neither creature utters its mournful note while it has enough, the ass in good pasture and the ox with provender before it; and if Job, in real want, made no moan at all, he would be more stupid and senseless than the brutes. He hears in it too an answer to the charge of inconsistency: in his prosperity he had been as silent as the well-fed ox, but now, in distress, he cannot but cry out, as those animals do when their food is gone — and he glances at the friends, who lived in tranquillity and so, like beasts with full mangers, had no occasion to grieve.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the natural history behind the image. The word for the wild ass is pere, the onager of the old versions, the same animal as the tame ass but, running wild, grown larger, stronger, and fleeter of foot. And he presses Job's point as a direct challenge to the friends: "You condemn me for complaining; do I complain without a cause?" The wild ass will not bray, nor the ox low, but in want; had Job been at rest and at ease, he too would have held his peace. John Wesley says the same in fewer words: even the brute beasts, when they have convenient food, are quiet and contented; it is therefore no wonder that the friends, living in ease and prosperity, complain not — any more than Job himself did while he wanted nothing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the figure into a defence of Job's altered temper. In his prosperity he did not bray over his grass nor low over his fodder; but now that he is utterly deprived of all his comforts, he must be a stock or a stone, and want the sense of an ox or a wild ass, if he did not give some vent to his grief. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the very instinct of a dumb creature — silent while fed, vocal in hunger — vindicates the sufferer: complaint wrung out by real anguish is not the mark of a fretful spirit but the honest cry of nature under a burden, and the friends, who have never felt that hunger, are in no position to wonder that he groans.
6:
The taste-images of this verse — "Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?" — divide the witnesses over what exactly Job finds so loathsome. The reformed John Gill gives both readings. Taken of his food, the point is plain: pulse and the like have no relish without salt, and things bitter and unpleasant are nauseated by men; no wonder, then, that the wormwood and water of gall on which Job is now fed should be so distasteful that he loathes it and complains. But some, he notes, apply the words to the speeches of Eliphaz — insipid, foolish talk, unsuitable and disagreeable to Job, not seasoned with the salt of prudence, grace, and goodness, and so as flat to him as an unsalted dish.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports a whole spread of construals and settles on Mr. Good's: does insipid food without salt, does the very white of an egg, give forth any pungency? That which has nothing sharp or irritating in it produces no irritation; so Job would be quiet and not complain if he had nothing acrimonious to bear — but, alas, the food he is doomed to eat is the very calamity most acute to his soul, that which he most loathes. Clarke records too the rival guesses, some rendering the phrase "the juice of purslain," others even "the drivel of dreams," and owns that the interpretations are many. John Wesley keeps the simplest sense: men complain of their meat when it is merely unsavoury; how much more when it is as bitter as Job's now is?

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, notes the same lexical doubt that troubled Clarke — that the words rendered "the white of an egg" are taken by some to mean the juice of purslain — while agreeing that the thrust is the same: Job's soul refuses to touch the tasteless remedies pressed upon it, as it would refuse loathsome meat. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry blends the two lines the others hold apart: the white of an egg is now the choicest dish at Job's impoverished table, and it stands as well for the friends' consolations, in themselves as sapless and insipid as that, and, when applied to his wounds, as loathsome and burdensome as the most sorrowful meat. The witnesses circle a single grievance without wholly agreeing on its object — whether it is the bitter portion God has served him, or the flavourless comfort his friends have brought — but all hear a man for whom nothing set before him, in providence or in counsel, has any savour left.
7:
This verse presses the taste-figure of the one before it to its bitter end — "The things that my soul refused to touch are as my sorrowful meat" — and the reformed John Gill again spreads before us the two ways it may be read. On the first, Job speaks of literal food: the things he once would not so much as touch with his fingers, let alone eat, are now his constant and only fare in his sorrowful circumstances; and Gill passes on the vivid gloss of some Jewish writers, that what Job formerly disdained even to wipe his hands with he is now glad to spread as a cloth upon which to eat his bread of sorrow — reduced so low that yesterday's refuse is today's table. On the second reading, which Gill plainly prefers, the "things" are the insipid and disagreeable words of his friends — their doctrines, instructions, and exhortations — which he refuses and rejects, and which he loathes and nauseates as he loathes his tainted food, meat gone corrupt and rotten, the very refuse of the table.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the verse in yet a third light, not of food nor of words but of the calamity itself: the sense, he suggests, is that those grievous afflictions which Job once dreaded even to think of are now his daily, though sorrowful, bread — the dreaded thing become the very diet of his life. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands close to Gill's first reading and draws a plain lesson from it: even that food which once Job would have scorned to touch he is now glad of, and it is his sorrowful meat; wherefore it is wisdom not to accustom ourselves or our children to be nice and dainty about meat and drink, since we know not how low we may be brought, nor how that which we now disdain may be made acceptable by necessity.

The witnesses do not so much divide as lay one image over another, and the verse gains from the layering. Whether the loathsome thing is the beggar's food Job must now swallow, or the tasteless comfort his friends keep offering, or the very stroke of affliction he once could not bear to imagine, the confession is the same: what his whole soul recoiled from has become his portion, set before him day after day, and he must feed on what he most abhors. It is the language of a man whose life has been so inverted that the intolerable is now the ordinary, and the witnesses let the single sentence carry the full weight of that reversal.
8:
The complaint now turns into a petition, and a startling one — "Oh that I might have my request; and that God would grant me the thing that I long for" — for the thing Job longs for is death. The reformed John Gill lingers on the wish that his request might "come": that it might go up and enter the ears of the Lord, or come back fulfilled into his own bosom; and he names the object plainly. Death is the one thing that lies uppermost in Job's mind, the single boon he is now most solicitous to obtain — death imagined almost as a person who looks in at the windows and comes into the houses of men.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the petition with a stern compassion. Ungoverned passion often grows more violent when it meets a rebuke, as the troubled sea rages most where it dashes against a rock: Eliphaz had checked Job for courting death, and now Job says it again, more vehemently than before. One would expect his longing to be that God would deliver and restore him; instead it is that God would destroy him. Yet Henry marks a crucial restraint — for all his impatience Job never offers to destroy himself, nor to take away his own life; the Stoic morals that recommend self-murder as a redress of grief were unknown to him and abhorrent to the law of God and nature. However uneasy the soul's confinement in the body, it must not break prison, but wait for a fair discharge; and so Job only begs that it may please God to do it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the ground of the wish: having no hope that he will ever be redeemed from his helpless state, Job earnestly asks God to shorten it by taking away his life. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the psychology in a wider frame. Baffled among his fellow-creatures, Job turns, like many another, to God as his only hope — though it is rather from God than in God that his hope lies; his is the common language of all sufferers who think relief must come through a change of circumstances rather than in themselves. So he looks to death as his one expectation and calls it the thing he longs for, when in truth, all unknown to him, there were with God many years of life and prosperity yet in store — a hope that in Job 17 will darken even further into blank hopelessness. Keil and Delitzsch fix the paradox at the centre of it all: this is the strange thing, that not life but death has become the object of his expectation. The witnesses do not divide; they hold the wish up as at once real, pitiable, and mistaken.
9:
Job spells out the request of the verse before — "Even that it would please God to destroy me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off" — and the reformed John Gill is careful to guard the word from being read as despair of his soul. Job does not ask for everlasting destruction of body and soul, which would be a terror to him; he asks only for the dissolution of the body, and that not its annihilation but its being crushed. The verb, Gill notes, means to bruise and beat to pieces; Job would have his house of clay broken to powder and returned to its original dust, so that Broughton fitly renders it "to bring me to the dust of death."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes the archery in "let loose his hand": it is the metaphor of a bowman drawing his arrow to the head and then loosing his hold, that the shaft may fly to the mark — the same figure of the divine arrows that opened Job's complaint in v.4. John Wesley reads the petition at its simplest: to destroy is to end his days and his calamities together. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it the soldier's mercy-stroke — Job asks God, who once let loose his hand to make him poor and then to make him sick, to let it loose once more to put an end to his life, the very blow that once, as a destruction from the Almighty, had been a terror to him in Job 31:23, now courted, yet in hope that the spirit should be saved.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording and its difficulty. Keil and Delitzsch take "cut me off" of the soul or life, the thread of life severed, comparing the like phrase in Isaiah 38:12, and note the piled optative verbs by which the wish is heaped up. Charles Ellicott confesses the sequence of thought here is obscure and uncertain: Job's meaning may be that, whatever befell him, his consolation would still be that he had never denied the words of the Holy One. The clause rendered "I would harden myself in sorrow" is, he warns, the most doubtful in the passage, occurring nowhere else in Scripture; some render "I would exult in pain that spareth not," others "Though I burn in sorrow," while "Let him not spare" or "Though he spare not" seems to him preferable. The witnesses do not divide over the substance — Job asks God to strike the final blow — but the grammatical-historical voices leave the reader honestly aware how much of the sufferer's speech trembles at the very edge of what the words can be made to bear.
10:
The wish for death carries its own consolation — "Then should I yet have comfort... for I have not concealed the words of the Holy One" — and the witnesses part company over both the middle clause and the ground of the hope. The reformed John Gill weighs whether the comfort is had before death or after. It may be the exultation of a man on the very brink of eternity, able amid all his pains to cry, "O death, where is thy sting?"; or it may be the comfort beyond the grave, for Job looks for no temporal comfort on this side of it — his substance, children, and health being gone past recovery — but for the presence of God and the fulness of joy after death.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke opens the textual question. Several manuscripts, with the Vulgate and the Chaldee, read not "yet" but "this" — "This should be my comfort" — the very expectation that God will make a speedy end being his joy. To "harden myself in sorrow" is, on Clarke's reading, to endure the present with a determinate resolution, knowing the misery has a term; and "let him not spare" means, let him use whatever means he will, for Job will not resist the decree of a God who is holy and just. John Wesley reads the same clauses as courage borrowed from hope: Job would bear up under all his torments with the prospect of death and of blessedness after death, asking God not to suffer him to live longer; and "I have not concealed the words of the Holy One" means he had steadfastly believed them and was never ashamed nor afraid boldly to profess and preach the true religion in the midst of the heathen — so that if God cut him off, he would be a gainer by it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes that clear conscience the whole foundation of the comfort. Job had the words of the Holy One committed to him, and it was his joy that he had not concealed them — not kept them from himself, stifling his convictions or imprisoning the truth in unrighteousness, nor kept them to himself, but had owned and communicated them; and those, and those only, may promise themselves comfort in death who are good and do good while they live. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the last word: to "conceal" is here to deny, and Job's confidence is the Psalmist's in Ps. 40:9-10, that he has not hid God's righteousness within his heart. Keil and Delitzsch render the trembling middle line "I would exult in unsparing pain," so that the confession stands unbroken — "that I have not disowned the words of the Holy One." The witnesses do not divide on the heart of it: whatever the exact rendering, Job grounds his one comfort not in his innocence of suffering but in his fidelity to God's word.
11:
Against Eliphaz's promise of recovery Job sets two despairing questions — "What is my strength, that I should hope? and what is mine end, that I should prolong my life?" — and the witnesses hear in them a man refusing the very comfort offered him. The reformed John Gill reads the first against the restoration of health that Eliphaz had held out: Job's strength is so broken that he cannot hope for it, and death is more desirable than a life stretched out in such weakness, pain, and sorrow; the word may also mean "that I should bear" so crushing a load, or that I should hold out and endure. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch put the same sense as a rhetorical whole: is not Job's strength already so wasted, and his unhappy end so certain, that a long calm waiting is at once impossible and useless? The phrase they render "prolong my life" is literally to draw out the soul — to spread and stretch the intensity of feeling, that is, to be patient.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, notes the same double possibility in the second clause: "prolong my life" is the literal rendering, but some understand it, as in our idiom of long-suffering, to mean "be patient" — to hold out under the strain. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the hopelessness home. Adam Clarke has Job say he can never suppose his strength will be restored, and that even were it possible he has no comfortable prospect of a happy end; the state of his body and of his affairs alike preclude all hope. John Wesley reads the strength as so spent that it is vain to look for the restitution Eliphaz had promised in Job 5:22; and he turns the second question to a different edge — "what is my end?" is to ask, what is death to me? It is not terrible but comfortable; why then should I wish to prolong my life? Yet, Wesley adds, as desirous of death as Job was, he never once offered to put an end to his own.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers both questions into a meditation on the frailty of all human strength. Job has no reason to expect long life, for his strength is a depending strength — no more than God gives — a decaying strength, daily spending its stock, and a disproportionate strength, that two or three days' sickness can make weak as water, so that instead of reckoning on length of days we should wonder we have lived until now. And he has no reason to desire it, for those who through grace are ready for another world can see little in this to invite their stay. The witnesses do not divide; they let Job's two questions stand as the reasoned despair of a man who finds in his own wasted body no ground either to hope for recovery or to wish it.
12:
Job measures his endurance against the hardest materials he can name — "Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?" — and the witnesses take the two questions as a proverbial confession of mere mortal frailty. The reformed John Gill fills out the figure: is Job's strength like that of foundation and corner stones that bear up a whole building, or like a stone pillar that can carry a prodigious weight? It is not; and therefore he cannot sustain the load laid upon him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same denial — are his muscles brass and his sinews steel? They are not; and so he cannot hold out always in this pain and misery, but must sink under it. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, states it plainly: Job is not made of stone or brass but of flesh and blood, as other men are, and is therefore unable to endure these miseries longer, and can neither hope for nor desire the continuance of his life.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enriches the verse with its long afterlife in the poets, for it is, he says, a proverbial saying that exists in all countries. He sets beside it Cicero's word that man is not chiselled out of the rock nor hewn out of the oak, but has a body and a soul, moved by mind and by the senses; and Homer's lines in the fourth book of the Iliad, where Apollo from the height of Troy urges on the Trojans — their enemies' bodies are not rock, nor ribbed with steel, but flesh into which weapons enter and strokes are felt. These, Clarke observes, are almost the same expressions as Job's, the common speech of suffering humanity insisting that it is made of penetrable stuff. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the couplet stand within the run of questions by which Job proves his helplessness, the flesh of brass and the strength of stones alike denied.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers force precisely from its obviousness. Job is not asking a real question but exposing the cruelty of the demand implied in the friends' counsel — that he should simply bear up, wait, and hope, as though he were built of something other than perishable flesh. To require of a man in his torment the patience of granite or the impassiveness of bronze is to forget what a man is; and the sufferer, by naming the stone and the brass he is not, quietly convicts his comforters of asking the impossible. It is a small verse, but the witnesses let it carry Job's whole protest against being measured by a strength no creature of flesh possesses.
13:
The section of self-defence ends on a question that the witnesses read in flatly opposite ways — "Is not my help in me? and is wisdom driven quite from me?" The reformed John Gill takes it as an assertion of resource still remaining: "my help," or "my defence," is in Job's own power, for though he has no strength to lift his outward burden, he has the testimony of a good conscience within him and the force of reason and argument on his side, and by these he can defend himself against the calumnies cast upon him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way, as Job's guard against the charge of raving: he has the use of his reason, and can help himself though the friends will not help him; wisdom is not driven from him; he is "not mad, most noble Eliphaz, but speaks the words of truth and soberness," for those who have grace in exercise have a light within that is their help in the worst of times. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, gives the affirmation its sharpest form: granting his outward condition is helpless and hopeless, has he therefore lost his understanding? Cannot he still judge whether it is better to live or to die, whether he is a hypocrite, whether the friends' words have any weight?

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, however, turn the question inside out, rendering it "Or am I then not utterly helpless, and continuance is driven from me?" — no longer a claim of inward resource but a confession of total collapse. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans the same way: his help is all in himself, and that, alas, is perfect weakness; the word he renders "subsistence," all that is stable and permanent, is driven quite from him — friends forsaken, property gone, and nothing left. Yet Clarke is emphatic on one point against a common misreading: Job does not say, and does not mean, that reason itself is driven from him; there is no mark in all this chapter of a mind deranged or impaired.

So the verse holds a real divide. Is Job insisting that, stripped of everything else, he still has help and wisdom enough within to plead his own cause — or is he owning that he is utterly without help, his last stay taken away? The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, feels the obscurity keenly and offers both: the sense may be "Is it not that I have no help in me, and wisdom is driven from me?" or "Is it because there is no help in me that therefore wisdom is driven far from me" by your reproaches? The witnesses agree only that the friends have driven Job to the question, and the reader is left to weigh, with them, whether it is the cry of a man who still holds his ground or of one who has lost it all but his innocence.
14:
Job turns from himself to his comforters, and the witnesses converge on a verse whose first half is clear and whose second is one of the book's true cruxes — "To him that is afflicted pity should be showed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty." The reformed John Gill dwells on the afflicted man as the natural object of pity, whether stricken inwardly with a sense of God's displeasure, or outwardly in body, substance, and kin, or beset by Satan or by men; and pity, he says, is no bare feeling but an inward sympathy expressed in deeds — visiting, speaking comfortably, relieving the need as ability allows — which is exactly what the law of friendship requires. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry grounds Job's expectation on common humanity: compassion is a debt owed to the afflicted, and inhumanity is impiety, for "he that withholds compassion from his friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty" — so the Chaldee reads it — since surely those have no fear of God's rod who feel nothing for those who smart under it, echoing the challenge of 1 John 3:17 and the pure religion of James 1:27.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the accusing clause the same way, of the pitiless friend. John Wesley paraphrases: "thou hast no pity for thy friend — a plain evidence that thou art guilty of the very thing thou chargest me with, the want of the fear of God." Adam Clarke prefers the Vulgate, "He who takes away mercy from his friend hath cast off the fear of the Lord," and adds a textual turn: where the received text has the word for "afflicted" — from a root meaning to waste or melt away — some two-and-thirty manuscripts read instead "to him that despiseth his friend," so that the line becomes, with Mr. Good, "Shame to the man who despiseth his friend! He indeed hath departed from the fear of the Almighty." Eliphaz, Clarke notes, had in effect despised Job, and well deserved the stroke.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott alone hesitates over who it is that forsakes the fear. It is difficult, he says, to fix the relation of dependent clauses in so archaic a tongue, and the Authorised rendering is at all events not correct; the sense may rather be "even to one that forsaketh the fear of the Almighty" — pity owed even to the ungodly — or, better still, "lest he should forsake" it, or "he may even forsake" it: that is, deny the afflicted man his due compassion and you may drive him to cast off his religion altogether. So the crux stands. On the common reading, followed by Henry, Wesley, and Clarke, the man who denies pity is the one who has abandoned the fear of God; on Ellicott's, the clause looks the other way, warning that unpitied misery may tempt the sufferer himself to let go his hold on God. The witnesses agree wholly on the duty — pity is owed — and divide only on where the peril of its refusal finally falls.
15:
Job opens the most celebrated image of the chapter, the winter torrent that fails in the heat — "My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook" — and the witnesses linger over both the word "brethren" and the figure it governs. The reformed John Gill notes that these brethren are the three friends, kin to Job not by blood or country but by their common profession of the one true and living God among an idolatrous people — a relation that only aggravates their treachery. He looked for them to condole and comfort; instead they reproached and grieved him, and so dealt deceitfully, like a brook fed not by a living spring but by the winter's rains and melting snows, that swells for a while into the show of a great river and then is gone. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the deceit as the frustrating of just expectations: they came by solemn appointment to mourn with him, and much was hoped from such wise and knowing men, but instead of oil they poured vinegar into his wounds — a warning, he says, that it is our wisdom to cease from man and to trust the rock of ages, not broken cisterns.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the natural picture. Adam Clarke describes the land torrents that appear suddenly and as suddenly vanish, bred by rains on the mountains in the wet season and swallowed again by the thirsty sands: at first they promise a lasting stream and are watched with delight, the tanks filled from them; sometimes they swell so large and rapid as to carry all before them, and then fail — so the friends had promised much sympathy and proved physicians of no value. John Wesley marks that though Eliphaz alone had spoken, the other two showed their approval, so all are "brethren" who dealt deceitfully by adding to the afflictions they had come to remove; it is no new thing, he adds, for even brethren to deal so, and therefore our wisdom to cease from man.

The grammatical-historical voices give the simile its geography and its grammar. Charles Ellicott calls it one of the most celebrated poetical figures in the book, carrying us into desert life, where the wadys, so mighty and torrent-like in winter, dwindle to insignificant streams or fail altogether in summer; he recalls seeing the great wady of the Guadalquivir at Cordova in August reduced to a third-rate current trickling in divided channels through its stony bed. Keil and Delitzsch, opening the description that runs to v.20, render the second line "as the stream of brooks they pass away," and note the disputed word that the moderns would point not as the "paths" of the torrents but as the caravans that travel by them — a reading that will matter as the picture unfolds. The witnesses do not divide: the friends are a dry wady, glittering when no one needs them and empty in the hour of thirst.
16:
The torrent is described first in its winter fulness — "which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid" — and the witnesses read the dark, swollen water partly as landscape and partly as a portrait of the friends. The reformed John Gill notes that streams frozen over take on a blackish colour, what men call a black frost; and he offers two applications. The words might describe Job and his household, in black and rueful circumstances under God's heavy hand; but Gill prefers to see in them the friends themselves — foul and troubled waters frozen hard, their true colour hidden under the ice, an image of the foulness of their spirits and the blackness of their hearts, however fair they appeared without. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the plain picture of the flood: the brooks make a great show when they are swollen with the waters of a land-flood, the melting of ice and snow, which leaves them blackish and muddy — the pretension matching the friends' large promise of comfort.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses attend to the physical process. Adam Clarke describes waters suddenly frozen, their very foam turned to the likeness of snow or hoar-frost; and when the heat comes they are speedily melted, while the evaporation above and the absorption of the thirsty sand below are so strong together that they soon vanish. John Wesley marks the irony of the season: in winter, when the traveller neither needs nor desires the water, the brooks are full, congealed by the frost, with the snow-water of former falls lying hidden beneath; for Job speaks not of brooks fed by a constant spring but of those filled only by the accidental falls of rain and snow.

The witnesses do not divide, and the detail carries more weight than its brevity suggests. The very fulness of these streams is the measure of their unreliability: they are blackest and heaviest precisely when they are needed least, gorged with ice and buried snow in the cold months when no thirsty man is on the road. The friends, so the figure runs, had made their darkest, most impressive show of feeling when Job's prosperity asked nothing of them; the store of sympathy seemed deep and abundant while the weather was cold. What such a brook will do when the heat comes and a man's life hangs on finding water in it, the next verses will tell — and the hidden snow that looks like a reserve will prove to be the very thing that fails soonest. The witnesses let the winter picture stand as a promise the summer will break.
17:
The turn of the seasons undoes the brook — "What time they wax warm, they vanish: when it is hot, they are consumed out of their place" — and the witnesses read the melting away as the exact figure of a friendship that fails at the moment of need. The reformed John Gill fixes the correspondence: the ice and snow that swelled the stream, when the weather turns warm, melt down and disappear; and just so his friends ceased to be friends in the day of adversity. When the sun of affliction had once looked upon him, they deserted him — or at the least they administered no comfort, drying up precisely as the water dried when the heat came on. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks the two stages of the ruin in the verse's own words: "they wax warm" as the weather grows milder, and they "vanish"; then comes the hot season, when running water is most refreshing and most necessary, and at that very hour they are consumed out of their place, gone from where the thirsty man had counted on finding them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the same line forward within their reading of the whole desert scene, rendering the second clause "it becometh hot, they are extinguished from their place" — the stream not merely shrinking but snuffed out where it lay, as a flame is put out. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral the picture presses toward: when those who were rich and high are sunk and impoverished and stand most in need of comfort, then the very people who once gathered thick about them stand aloof, and those who before had commended them are forward to run them down.

The witnesses do not divide, and even with few voices the verse yields its point cleanly. The failure is not gradual neglect but a vanishing timed with cruel exactness to the heat — the friendship evaporates just as the sun rises highest and the traveller's thirst grows sharpest. What in the cold had seemed a full and reliable channel proves, when the burning day arrives, to hold nothing at all; the water is not low but wholly gone, "consumed out of their place," as though it had never been. So Job's comforters, abundant in sympathy while he had no need of it, are found utterly dry the instant his need is real. The figure is the more bitter for being so natural: everyone who has crossed a summer desert knows the dry bed where a winter torrent ran, and Job has made his friends that bed.
18:
The vanished stream leaves a trackless waste behind it — "The paths of their way are turned aside; they go to nothing, and perish" — and here the witnesses genuinely divide over what it is that turns aside and is lost. The reformed John Gill reads it of the waters: when melted, they run off in little streams and windings, this way and that, until they are wholly lost and not a trace of their channel can be found; so every appearance of the friends' friendship is gone, with no track of it remaining. The wesleyan-arminian voices agree. Adam Clarke observes that such torrents sometimes forsake their ancient channels — a thing frequent with the Ganges — and, dividing into ever smaller streams, come to nothing and perish, utterly swallowed in the sands. John Wesley says the same: they are gone out of their channel, flowing hither and thither till they are quite consumed.

The grammatical-historical witnesses, however, suspect the verse looks not at the water but at the travellers who trusted it. Keil and Delitzsch would point the disputed word not as the "paths" of the torrents but as the caravans, and render the line so that these turn about from their course, march up into the trackless waste, and perish — deceived, that is, by the streams they had reckoned on. Charles Ellicott lays both possibilities side by side and owns the doubt: it is uncertain whether the words apply to the streams or to the caravans — "the paths of their way are turned aside and come to nought," or "the caravans that travel by the way of them turn aside, and go into the waste and perish" — but he judges the next verse, with its troops of Tema, to make the second the more probable.

The two readings are not, in the end, far apart, for they meet in a single catastrophe. Whether it is the brook that wanders off and dies in the sand, or the thirsty company that follows the brook's remembered course only to wander off and die themselves, the deceit is the same and the ruin is the same: the promise of water draws men out of their safe road and then dissolves, leaving them to turn about in a waste that has nothing to give. The witnesses leave the ambiguity standing, as the Hebrew leaves it; and the very blurring of stream and searcher deepens the figure, for Job's friends are at once the failed torrent and the cause of his own straying hope. What the caravans do at the water's grave, the verse that follows will show.
19:
The picture widens from the dry bed to the thirsty travellers who came seeking it — "The troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them" — and the witnesses fill in the desert geography and the merchants' hope. The reformed John Gill identifies Tema as a city of Arabia named from a son of Ishmael, and the troops as trading caravans that, passing that way, would look toward the places where in winter they had seen great sheets of water frozen and snow-covered, counting on them to supply their thirst in the summer heat. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses sharpen the scene. Adam Clarke has the caravans of Tema arrive full of expectation at the very spots where torrents were known to descend, hoping not only to slake their thirst but to fill their water-skins — only to find the waters wholly dissipated and lost; and the companies of Sheba waited for them in vain, and were confounded. John Wesley notes that Tema and Sheba lay in the hot, dry country of Arabia, where water was scarce and therefore precious to travellers, who journeyed not singly, as we do, but in companies, for security against wild beasts and robbers.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the learning of the geographers. Citing Fürst, he places Tema as a tract in the north of the Arabian desert, on the borders of the Syrian, where traffic passed by caravan from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, and he gathers the other Scriptures that name it in Isaiah 21:14 and Jeremiah 25:23; Sheba he takes for a district on the Arabian Gulf, whose merchants trafficked with the distant cities of the East and enriched themselves with plunder, as the Sabeans had already done to Job in Job 1:15. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet in the same sense — the travelling bands of Tema looked, the caravans of Saba hoped, for the streams — so that the whole weight of expectation is laid on water that is not there.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gives the simile its human centre. It is no longer merely a brook that fails but a company of living men, strung out across the burning waste, straining their eyes toward a remembered gleam of water and pinning their lives on it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the very murmur of their hope — "a little further," says one, "when I last came this way there was water enough" — and it is exactly this confident, remembered expectation that Job means. He had looked toward his friends as the parched caravan looks toward the wady; the more sure the hope, as the witnesses show, the more crushing the discovery at the verse that follows.
20:
The caravans reach the water's grave, and their hope turns to shame — "They were confounded because they had hoped; they came thither, and were ashamed." The reformed John Gill draws the scene to its bitter close: coming at last to the places where they had counted on finding water and finding none, the travellers are confounded, ashamed of their vain hope, and left to reflect with self-reproach on the folly of building expectation on so groundless a surmise. The very confidence with which they had journeyed becomes the measure of their humiliation when the bed proves dry. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the two clauses in turn: they had "hoped," that is, comforted themselves along the way with the expectation of water; and they were "ashamed," as men who have deceived both themselves and others. Wesley turns it at once into a warning — we prepare confusion for ourselves by our vain hopes, and the reeds we lean on break precisely because we lean on them.

The grammatical-historical witnesses set the disappointment in the wider language of Scripture. Charles Ellicott compares the confusion here to Jeremiah's picture of the famine, where the nobles send their little ones to the waters and they come to the empty pits and return with their vessels empty, ashamed and confounded and covering their heads, in Jeremiah 14:3. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect — disappointed on account of their trust, they came thus far and were red with shame — the blush of baffled expectation staining the faces of men who had trusted and been failed.

The witnesses do not divide, and the completed simile now lies open. Job has said, in effect, that his three friends are not merely unhelpful but a positive deception: like the winter wady that glitters in the cold and vanishes in the heat, they raised in him a hope proportioned to their show, and then, when his need reached its height, they had nothing to give. The shame the caravans feel is the shame of misplaced trust, and Job means his comforters to feel the sting of it — that they came to him with all the ceremony of sympathy and proved, at the crisis, an empty channel. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson the whole figure has been driving toward: the greater men's confidence in the creature, the greater their confusion when it fails; and it is wiser to make God our confidence, who never sends the thirsty soul away ashamed.
21:
Job at last drops the figure and names the friends directly — "For now ye are nothing; ye see my casting down, and are afraid" — and the witnesses gather around a genuine textual crux at the heart of the line. The reformed John Gill explains that the friends once seemed something to Job — men he thought wise, good, and tender-hearted — but in his distress they prove nothing to him, no comfort at all. He notes the two readings: as the text stands, "ye are nothing"; but the margin has "ye are to it," that is, ye are become like it, the deceitful brook just described, which is how Jarchi takes it. Broughton, he adds, happily unites both — "so now ye are become like that, even nothing" — for as that torrent is of no use to the fainting traveller, so the friends are of no use to Job.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same variant with care. The reading wavers between two forms distinguished only by a letter, the Keri directing one and the written text the other; the Keri, they judge, yields no suitable sense, whereas the written word, taken as a noun of negation, gives exactly the point — "ye are become nothing; your friendship proves itself equal to nothing." The Targum, following the written text, renders it "ye are become as though ye had never been." Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, records both possibilities without forcing a choice: "Surely now ye are become like it," that wady, or, on the reading the Authorised Version follows, "ye have become nothing — ye have seen an object of terror, and are terrified; ye have seen my broken-down condition, and are dismayed at it."

On the second half of the verse the wesleyan-arminian witnesses fasten with feeling. Adam Clarke paraphrases: the friends are to Job just what the deceitful torrents were to the caravans of Tema and Sheba — nothing; they see him hurried from his eminence into want and misery, and instead of drawing near to comfort him they start back, terrified at his calamity. John Wesley hears the same recoil, and probes its motive: they are shy of him and afraid for themselves, dreading either that some further plague should fall and involve them, or that the ruined man should become a burden they must bear. The witnesses do not divide on the sense, however they settle the letter: whether the friends have become "nothing" or become "like" the failed brook, they amount to the same, a comfort that recoils in fear at the very sight of the misery it was called to relieve.
22:
Job now turns the tables and asks what he had ever demanded of these friends that should make them recoil — "Did I say, Bring unto me? or, Give a reward for me of your substance?" The reformed John Gill puts the question simply: did Job ever invite them to come bringing presents in their hands to support him in his necessitous state? He had asked no such thing. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this the first of the pleas by which Job both justifies himself and convicts his friends. Though needy, he was not craving nor burdensome — and those whose troubles serve them to beg by are commonly less pitied than the silent poor. Job would gladly see his friends, but he never said "Bring unto me," nor put them to any expense; he did not urge them to make a collection to set him up again in the world, though his losses had come by the hand of God and not by his own folly, though he was utterly impoverished, and though in his better days he had himself been charitable to those in distress. A good man, Henry observes, when troubled himself, is afraid of being troublesome to his friends, as Paul worked with his hands that he might not be burdensome to any.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the reproach gently. Adam Clarke has Job ask why they stand aloof: has he demanded presents of them, or asked to be supplied out of their stores? John Wesley hears him say that he never asked them to give him anything for his support or relief — they might at least have given him comfortable words, when he expected nothing else from them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott spells out the argument folded into the question: it is not as though Job had abused their former kindness; he never laid himself under any obligation to them, never asked their help before. Had he done so, he might have worn out their patience and so justly brought upon himself their present harshness — but of that they cannot convict him.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, open here the run of verses in which Job challenges the friends to name his fault, taking "Bring unto me" and "give a reward of your substance" as the first of the things he never sought. The witnesses do not divide, and the thrust of the verse is one. Job's want had laid no claim on their purses; he had begged neither gift nor ransom; and this makes their coldness the more inexcusable, for they drew back as though from a suppliant who would drain them, when in truth he had asked them for nothing but the sympathy any afflicted man may look for from a friend. The very modesty of his need, the witnesses agree, is what turns their fear and their reproaches into so plain an unkindness.
23:
Job completes the list of the things he never asked — "Or, Deliver me from the enemy's hand? or, Redeem me from the hand of the mighty?" — and the witnesses read the two verbs as the two ways one great man might have begged another's help. The reformed John Gill notes that the phrase for "the enemy" may be rendered "the hand of straitness," the tribulation and difficulty that pressed Job on every side; he had not summoned the friends to rescue him from that. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses distinguish the means implied in the two words. John Wesley takes "deliver" of rescue by force of arms — as Abraham armed his servants and delivered Lot — and "redeem" of ransom by price; Job had asked neither a war waged on his behalf nor a sum paid to buy him back. Adam Clarke reads the enemies as the destroyers of Job's property: did he send for the friends to come and avenge him of the Sabeans and Chaldeans, or to recover his substance out of their hands? He had done no such thing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fills in the plunder that lay behind the question. Job did not urge his friends to raise the country in order to recover his cattle from the marauders, or to make reprisals upon them; "Did I send for you to deliver me out of the hand of the mighty? No," Henry has him say — "I never expected you either to expose yourselves to any danger or to put yourselves to any charge on my account. I will rather sit down content under my affliction than sponge upon my friends." Keil and Delitzsch let the couplet stand as the second and third of the demands Job never made, deliverance from the foe and redemption from the tyrant alike being things he had left unasked.

The witnesses do not divide, and the accumulating force of the questions is their point. Job had made upon these men no claim at all — not of gift, not of ransom, not of rescue by arms; he had not laid a finger on their wealth, their safety, or their ease. He asked, as the witnesses have shown, only for the pity that costs nothing but a kind look and a kind word. That so modest and so unpurchased a request should have been met with suspicion and reproach is the injustice the verse exposes; and by naming, one after another, the burdensome things he might have demanded and did not, Job leaves his comforters no excuse of self-defence to hide behind. Their coldness cannot be dressed up as prudence, for there was nothing to be prudent against.
24:
Having denied that he ever demanded anything of them, Job now offers the one thing he does ask — instruction — "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred." The reformed John Gill reads it as the mark of a humble and open mind. Having made his defence, Job would show that he is not stubborn nor unteachable, but ready to receive correction; for good men are desirous of being taught, of God and of men, not thinking themselves too wise for instruction, willing to learn from superiors, equals, and even inferiors — as Job here from friends who had used him unkindly. And he promises his silence: while they speak he will not interrupt nor contradict, but listen patiently, weigh what they say, and, if convinced, hold his peace. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same readiness to yield: Job is not obstinate but prepared to strike sail to truth the moment it is made to appear; if, instead of invidious reflections and uncharitable insinuations, they will give him plain instruction and solid argument, he is ready to acknowledge his error and own himself in a fault.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses hear the challenge in the offer. Adam Clarke has Job say, "Show me where I am mistaken; bring proper arguments to convince me of my errors, and you will soon find that I shall gladly receive your counsels and abandon the mistakes of which I am convicted." John Wesley compresses it: teach me — that is, convince me by solid arguments — and I will patiently hear and gladly receive your counsel. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect, "Teach me, and I will be silent, and cause me to understand wherein I have failed" — the promise of silence bound fast to the condition of real instruction.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they set the terms on which alone Job will be quiet. He does not claim to be beyond error; he asks only to be shown it, and shown it by argument rather than by insinuation. The offer is at once humble and shrewd, for it exposes the emptiness of what the friends have so far given: they have condemned him without convicting him, censured his words without pointing to a single sin. Job's willingness to be taught, the witnesses agree, is the very thing that turns the demand back on his accusers — let them make good their charge, and he will fall silent; but a vague reproach that names no fault has nothing in it to hold the tongue of an honest man. The next verse presses exactly that point, weighing what true instruction is against what the friends have offered in its place.
25:
Job draws the contrast between honest argument and mere censure — "How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?" — and the witnesses divide, as it happens, over the very word "forcible." The reformed John Gill takes "right words" for words according to right reason, strong and weighty arguments — "bony" arguments, as the Hebrew suggests — that carry conviction and bear men down; and pre-eminently the words of God, the Scriptures of truth, which are right because, though above right reason, they are never contrary to it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that a well-constructed argument resting on truth is irresistible, but turns the second clause into a rebuke: "what reproof is there in a reproof from you?" — having proved no fault, they have consequently reproved no vice. Clarke notes too a variant: where the received text reads "how forcible," two manuscripts with the Chaldee and some rabbins read "how savoury" or pleasant; both senses are good, though he keeps the common one. John Wesley states the plain point: words of truth have a marvellous power, but there is no truth in the friends' assertions nor weight in their arguments.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh that same alternative reading at length. The word might, they allow, bear the sense of the kindred term in Ps. 119:103 — "how smooth, how sweet are right words" — as Hirzel, Ewald, and Schlottmann would have it; but that meaning will not suit the way the root is used elsewhere in the book. They survey and set aside the rival construals — Hupfeld's "however bitter," Hahn's attempt to make it "how bad are right words" — finding none of them a clean fit, and so leave the force of the line contested. Charles Ellicott renders it "How forcible are words of uprightness! but what doth your reproof reprove?" and hears behind it the proverb that open rebuke is better than secret love: Job would sooner be honestly and openly corrected than subjected to the insinuations that pass among the friends for friendship.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the contrast into a maxim: fair reasoning has a commanding power, and it is a wonder if men are not conquered by it, whereas railing and foul language are impotent and only harden. The friends' whole management, he says, is weak — their hypothesis false, their surmises groundless, their application peevish. The witnesses do not finally divide over Job's meaning, however they settle the disputed word: true words, whether one calls them "forcible" or "sweet," have a power to persuade that the friends' reproaches wholly lack, for a rebuke that convicts of no fault reproves nothing at all. What such empty reproof amounts to, the next verse will say outright.
26:
Job exposes the poverty of the friends' method — that they fasten on his words rather than on his life — "Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?" The reformed John Gill hears a double thrust. Do they think to run him down with bare words, a parcel of talk without force of reasoning? Or is their whole device to catch at some words of his, uttered in distress, and make him an offender for a phrase — having no fact of his life to charge, they would support the accusation of hypocrisy and irreligion out of a few hasty expressions. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way: it is some expression let fall in his hurry, under the pressure of unprecedented affliction, that they catch at; they can find no flaw in his conduct, and would make him an offender for a word — why take such advantage of a man who complains in the bitterness of his heart, through despair of life? John Wesley adds the plea for allowance: do they think it enough to quarrel with some of his words, making no allowance for human infirmity or extreme misery? The speeches are those of a poor, miserable, hopeless man, and are "as wind," which passes away and is forgotten.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the unreasonableness of it. Charles Ellicott has Job say it cannot be their real intent to reprove mere words — words which he himself confesses to be rash, back in v.3, and which they seem to count as nothing better; if so, such words are hardly worth the trouble bestowed on them, and might be left to answer themselves. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse with a like edge: "Do you think to reprove words? the words of one in despair belong to the wind" — spoken to the air, not to be gathered up and weighed as if they were considered doctrine.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry states the principle at stake. The friends contrive, with a great deal of art, to reprove some passionate expressions of a man in a desperate condition, as though they were certain marks of reigning impiety and atheism; but a little candour and charity would have served to excuse them and put a better construction on them. Shall a man's whole spiritual state, Henry asks, be judged by some rash and hasty words that a surprising trouble has extorted from him? The witnesses do not divide: they agree that to arraign a sufferer's faith on the strength of words wrung from him by anguish is neither fair nor just, and that the friends, unable to convict Job's life, have fallen back on convicting his grief. What such tactics reveal about the friends themselves, the next verse will not spare to say.
27:
Job's protest reaches its sharpest point, charging the friends not merely with unkindness but with cruelty toward the helpless — "Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig a pit for your friend." The reformed John Gill takes the fatherless to be Job himself, stripped of children and substance and health, and, worse, deprived for a while of the felt presence of his heavenly Father, given over into Satan's hand; and he notes that the verb may be "ye cause to fall upon the fatherless" — whether their wrath, or a crushing weight, or, as Broughton has it, a net to entrap him in his talk. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads "overwhelm the fatherless" as a proverbial phrase for the most barbarous and inhuman conduct, the trampling of those who cannot defend themselves; Job, a childless father, thought himself as exposed to insult as any orphan, and had reason to resent it. To "dig a pit for your friend," Henry adds, is to ensnare under the colour of friendship: coming to sit with him, they invited his free speech, and then made his freedom the trap by which they caught him.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the two clauses in the same received sense. Adam Clarke has Job say that he is as destitute as the most miserable orphan — would they overwhelm such a one? — and that to dig a pit is to lay wait for him and entangle him in his words. John Wesley glosses "overwhelm" as to load with censures and calumnies, and "the fatherless" as one desolate, deprived of children, estate, and friends: Job spoke all he thought, as to friends, and they took occasion from it to cast him down.

The grammatical-historical voices, however, prefer a different rendering that keeps the poetic parallel. Charles Ellicott judges the sense to be rather "Ye would cast lots upon the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend" — more in accordance with the language, he says, and preserving the balance of the two lines. Keil and Delitzsch render it to the same effect: "ye would even cast lots for the orphan, and traffic about your friend." On this reading the charge is not only of overwhelming the weak but of coldly trading in him, gambling for the orphan's person and bartering away a friend as a piece of goods. The witnesses do not divide on the force of the accusation — that the friends have dealt with a broken man as the ruthless deal with the defenceless — but they differ on its image, whether Job pictures himself as an orphan crushed and pitted, or as a helpless prize the friends would cast lots for and sell. Either way, the verse marks the lowest point of his reproach, from which, in the verses that follow, he turns to plead once more for a fair hearing.
28:
From reproach Job turns to appeal, asking the friends to look him full in the face — "Now therefore be content, look upon me; for it is evident unto you if I lie." The reformed John Gill catches the courtesy of the opening: "be content" is "may it now please you," a respectful entreaty that they would look on him favourably, entertain better thoughts of him, and give his case a fresh and friendly hearing; for Job does not doubt that, so heard, he would be acquitted and his cause found righteous. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same request: view me, consider my circumstances, compare my words, and you must be convinced that I have spoken nothing but the truth. John Wesley presses it as a demand for better judgment — look upon my cause more carefully than you have, that you may give a more righteous verdict; do but look, and you will plainly discover where the truth lies.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the exact force of the looking. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse "be pleased to observe me keenly; I will not indeed deceive you to your face," and note that the word for observing means to scrutinize, to fasten the eye searchingly upon a thing; Job invites the closest inspection because he has nothing to hide about the reality and strangeness of his suffering. Charles Ellicott renders the second clause to the same point — "for surely I shall not lie to your face" — a man who dares to be watched so narrowly is a man conscious of no falsehood.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out what the friends would in fact see if they looked. "What do you see in me," he has Job ask, "that bespeaks me either a madman or a wicked man? Look in my face, and you may discern the indications of a patient and submissive spirit, for all this — that though I have cursed my day, I do not curse my God." Or, Henry adds, take the words more literally: look upon my ulcers and my sore boils, and by them it will be evident that I do not lie — that is, that I do not complain without cause, nor make my condition worse than it is. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job, so far from shrinking from scrutiny, courts it, staking his honesty on being seen; and the very confidence with which he offers himself to their eyes is his answer to men who had judged him without truly looking at all. Having asked to be seen, he asks in the next verse to be heard again, and judged afresh.
29:
Job asks the friends to reopen the case they had thought closed — "Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity; yea, return again, my righteousness is in it." The reformed John Gill offers two occasions for the word. It may be a plea that they return from their ill opinion and hard censures to juster sentiments; or, more literally, the friends may have been rising, as men do, to break off and leave, and Job entreats them to return to their seats, resume the debate, and hear his cause out. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as a call to a rehearing: consider the matter over again, without prejudice and partiality, and let not the result be an unrighteous sentence; and you will find, Job says, that my righteousness is in it — I am in the right in this matter, and though I cannot keep my temper as I should, I keep my integrity. A just cause, Henry observes, desires nothing more than a just hearing, and if need be a re-hearing.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the appeal for reconsideration in the same spirit. Adam Clarke has Job say, reconsider the whole subject, do not be offended, look again — "my righteousness is in it," that is, my very argumentation is a sufficient proof of my innocence. John Wesley glosses "return" as turn from your former judgment, and takes the middle clause as "let there be no iniquity in my words," while "my righteousness" means that in this cause between the friends and himself the right is on Job's side.

The grammatical-historical voices sharpen the wording. Keil and Delitzsch insist the challenging imperative is not "retrace your steps" but "begin afresh": try the case over again, let there be no injustice, for Job's righteousness still stands. Charles Ellicott renders it to the same effect — do not regard the case as settled, but come again and examine it, and try once more before you decide that there is any unrighteousness in Job, or, as he adds, in Job's tongue, a sense the pronoun here anticipates and the next verse will make explicit. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job is not asking for mercy but for justice — for a second, unprejudiced hearing in which the very act of honest examination will, he is sure, vindicate him. It is the confidence of a man who fears not scrutiny but the refusal of it; and it carries him straight into the closing challenge of the chapter, where he stakes everything on whether there is iniquity in his speech.
30:
The chapter ends on Job's boldest claim, that his own moral sense is still sound enough to know right speech from wrong — "Is there iniquity in my tongue? cannot my taste discern perverse things?" The reformed John Gill takes "iniquity in my tongue" of Job's words, whether those with which he cursed the day of his birth or those with which he charged his friends with unkindness; yet he adds the sober qualification that in itself the tongue is a world of iniquity, and the best of men are apt to offend both God and man in word. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the two questions as a plea of honesty backed by conscience: am I not an honest man? If in my haste my tongue had uttered anything false, would not my own conscience discern it — and would such a man as I knowingly defend what he knew to be wrong? Clarke closes his comment by calling the whole chapter an inimitable apology and defence of Job's conduct, which might have ended the controversy, had not the friends already prejudged his cause and resolved to bring him in guilty whatever he said.

John Wesley reads the verse in the same key, glossing "iniquity" as any untruth in what Job has said or shall yet say, and "taste" as his judgment, the faculty that tries words and actions as the palate tries its meats — a power he claims is still unimpaired in him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns the second question against the friends' condescension: they appear to think Job wholly incapable of judging his own cause because it is his own; but let them return in due course and they will find that he knows what is right as well as they, and that there is no more vicious reasoning in him than in them — probably less. Is his taste, he asks, so perverted that it cannot perceive what is perverse?

Ellicott adds a candid word on the difficulty every reader feels here: it is hard to draw out Job's argument in the logical form of Western thought, and harder still to trace the thread of it running on from one chapter to the next; look at the speech in detail and one is apt to lose the connection, yet it is just this connecting thread that is so difficult to detect and retain. The witnesses do not divide. They leave Job at the close of his reply exactly where his self-defence has aimed throughout — not claiming to have suffered without complaint, but claiming that his complaint is honest, his conscience clear, and his judgment sound; and by ending on the image of the discerning palate he binds the whole chapter together, for the man whose soul refused the tasteless comfort of his friends insists that the same taste can still tell the wholesome word from the perverse. The reply is finished, and the case, as Ellicott says, remains open only because the friends have determined not to close it in Job's favour.
